questions.answer: Keep \(\mathbb R^1\) unchanged: \((1,2,5)\). Compute the new second row: \(\mathbb R^2\) - 3R1 = \((3,7,20)\) - 3\((1,2,5)\) = [3 - 3, 7 - 6, 20 - 15] = \((0,1,5)\). Therefore the new matrix is \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2&5\\0&1&5\end{pmatrix}\).

The operation \(\mathbb R^1\) <-> \(\mathbb R^2\) swaps the two rows. The old second row becomes the first row, and the old first row becomes the second row. Therefore the result is \(\begin{pmatrix}1&-1&3\\0&2&4\end{pmatrix}\).
Keep \(\mathbb R^1\) unchanged. Multiply every entry of \(\mathbb R^2\) by 1/4: (1/4)\((0,4,8)\) = \((0,1,2)\). Therefore the result is \(\begin{pmatrix}1&0&2\\0&1&2\end{pmatrix}\).

Rows 1 and 2 stay unchanged. Compute the new third row: \(\mathbb R^3\) + 2R1 = \((-2,4,5)\) + 2\((1,-1,0)\) = [-2 + 2, 4 - 2, 5 + 0] = \((0,2,5)\). Therefore the new matrix is \(\begin{pmatrix}1&-1&0\\0&1&3\\0&2&5\end{pmatrix}\).

questions.prompt: Which elementary row operation would turn \(\begin{pmatrix}2&1&5\\6&4&17\end{pmatrix}\) into \(\begin{pmatrix}2&1&5\\0&1&2\end{pmatrix}\)?
questions.answer: The first row stays unchanged, so only \(\mathbb R^2\) changes. To eliminate the 6 under the leading 2, subtract 3 times \(\mathbb R^1\) from \(\mathbb R^2\). Compute \(\mathbb R^2\) - 3R1 = \((6,4,17)\) - \((6,3,15)\) = \((0,1,2)\). Therefore the operation is \(\mathbb R^2\) <- \(\mathbb R^2\) - 3R1.

questions.prompt: Apply the two operations \(\mathbb R^2\) <- \(\mathbb R^2\) - 2R1, then \(\mathbb R^3\) <- \(\mathbb R^3\) + \(\mathbb R^1\) to \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2&1\\2&5&4\\-1&0&3\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.answer: Start with \(\mathbb R^2\) <- \(\mathbb R^2\) - 2R1: \((2,5,4)\) - 2\((1,2,1)\) = \((0,1,2)\). Next apply \(\mathbb R^3\) <- \(\mathbb R^3\) + \(\mathbb R^1\) using the unchanged \(\mathbb R^1\): \((-1,0,3)\) + \((1,2,1)\) = \((0,2,4)\). The final matrix is \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2&1\\0&1&2\\0&2&4\end{pmatrix}\).

questions.prompt: Explain why multiplying one row by 0 is not an elementary row operation.
questions.answer: An elementary row scaling operation may multiply a row by a non-zero scalar only. Multiplying by 0 destroys the information in the row and cannot be reversed. Because row operations used for solving systems must preserve the solution set, multiplying a row by 0 is not allowed.

Compute the new first row: \(\mathbb R^1\) + 5R2 = \((1,-5,7)\) + 5\((0,1,-2)\) = [1, -5 + 5, 7 - 10] = \((1,0,-3)\). Keep \(\mathbb R^2\) unchanged. The result is \(\begin{pmatrix}1&0&-3\\0&1&-2\end{pmatrix}\).

questions.prompt: Find k so that applying \(\mathbb R^2\) <- \(\mathbb R^2\) + kR1 to \(\begin{pmatrix}2&1&0\\6&5&1\end{pmatrix}\) makes the first entry of \(\mathbb R^2\) equal to 0.
questions.answer: The first entry of the new \(\mathbb R^2\) is 6 + k*2. We want this to equal 0, so 6 + 2k = 0. Subtract 6 to get 2k = -6, hence \(k=-3\). Therefore use \(\mathbb R^2\) <- \(\mathbb R^2\) - 3R1.

questions.prompt: A learner changes \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\4&5&6\end{pmatrix}\) to \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\4&5&0\end{pmatrix}\) by altering only the final entry. Explain why this is not a valid row operation.
questions.answer: Elementary row operations act on whole rows: swap rows, scale a whole row by a non-zero scalar, or add a multiple of one whole row to another whole row. Changing only one entry does not fit any of these allowed operations. It can change the solution set arbitrarily, so it is not a valid row operation.
